title: Histomorphometric and morphological comparison after augmentation of extraction sockets with two different bone substitute materials in a split-mouth design after defined periods
summary:
When a tooth is extracted, a cavity remains in the jawbone. This usually heals within about three months, but during this time, some bone loss typically occurs. This bone resorption can make further treatment—such as placing a dental implant—more difficult, especially in the visible front tooth area.

To prevent bone loss, the empty socket can be filled with a special bone substitute material immediately after the extraction. This technique is called socket preservation. The goal is to maintain the original shape and volume of the bone as much as possible.

In the planned study, two different bone substitute materials will be compared: one of porcine origin (from pigs) and one of bovine origin (from cows). Both materials will be used in different areas of the same patient’s mouth (a “split-mouth” design).

The healing process will be monitored regularly using an oral scanner to precisely measure any changes in bone volume. Later, when the implant is placed, a small bone sample will be taken and analyzed in the laboratory to assess the quality of the newly formed bone.
